full_title: ATTY. PABLO B. FRANCISCO, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. MIGUEL S. ASUNCION, PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 99, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, ANTIPOLO CITY, RIZAL, RESPONDENT.
docket: A.M. No. RTJ-26-119 (formerly JIB FPI No. 21-076-RTJ)
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Undue delay in rendering a decision as simple neglect of duty (Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC)
Three-month period to decide for lower courts (Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 15(1)) and the duty to ask for an extension
Excuses for delay: heavy caseload, pandemic, executive judge duties
Prior administrative liability as an aggravating circumstance
No separate liability as a lawyer absent corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of rules

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VI. Judicial Department > E. The Supreme Court > 1. Composition, Powers, and Functions > b. Administrative Supervision over Lower Courts

doctrine:
**Undue delay in rendering a decision is a form of negligence that may be gross neglect of duty (a serious charge) or simple neglect of duty (a less serious charge) under Rule 140 of the Rules of Court, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC.** Lower courts must decide cases within three months from submission (Article VIII, Section 15(1), 1987 Constitution), and judges must deliver reserved decisions efficiently, fairly and with reasonable promptness (Canon 6, Section 5, New Code of Judicial Conduct). **A judge who cannot meet the period must ask the Court, through the OCA, for an extension** (OCA Circular No. 243-2022). Heavy caseload, the pandemic, duties as executive or assisting judge, and family health concerns do not excuse the delay when the judge never sought an extension and decided long after regular court operations resumed. Deciding the case later does not erase liability, and the judge cannot avoid the charge by saying the complainant should have appealed: the issue is the delay, not the merits (reiterated).

Simple neglect of duty is punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 but not exceeding PHP 100,000 (Rule 140, Section 15(b), in relation to Section 17(2)). A previous administrative liability for which a penalty was imposed is an aggravating circumstance (Section 19), allowing a penalty of up to double the maximum (Section 20). The complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence. The judge is not separately liable as a member of the Bar for the same delay without evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules.
facts:
Atty. Pablo Francisco was the plaintiff in Civil Case No. 12-9697, an action to annul a TCT filed on June 14, 2012 in the RTC of Antipolo City, Branch 99, presided over by Judge Miguel Asuncion. The defendants and their counsel failed to attend mediation, JDR, pre-marking and pre-trial, so the Pre-Trial Order of June 21, 2018 deemed their right to participate waived and allowed Atty. Francisco to present evidence ex parte. He finished presenting evidence on November 8, 2018, filed his written offer of exhibits on November 19, 2018, and filed his memorandum on December 10, 2018. On April 11, 2019, the judge admitted all his exhibits except Exhibit "G."

Atty. Francisco filed a Motion for a Decision on January 7, 2020, a Motion to Transfer Case to Another Sala on February 21, 2020, and a Motion for Inhibition dated August 19, 2020. The judge acted on none of them. Atty. Francisco then filed an administrative complaint dated August 20, 2021 for neglect of duty. The Judicial Integrity Board (JIB) required the judge to comment on November 16, 2021, and again on April 20, 2023, when it also directed him to show cause why he should not be disciplined as a member of the Bar.

In his Comment dated April 20, 2023, Judge Asuncion apologized and blamed the delay on the "influx of equally important matters." He had served as executive judge from October 16, 2020 to November 3, 2022, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, acting on search warrant and bail applications and attending meetings and courtesy calls with local offices. He was also assigned in January 2021 as assisting judge to help decongest caseloads, including in a newly created branch; his court had a new branch clerk of court; and he had family health concerns. He reported that he had decided the case on March 24, 2023, dismissing it for lack of cause of action, and argued that an administrative complaint is not the remedy against an adverse decision. The records showed that he had previously been reprimanded for undue delay (RTJ-20-2592) and had four more pending complaints for delay.

The Office of the Executive Director of the JIB recommended a fine of PHP 50,000 for simple neglect of duty and a fine of PHP 18,000 for violating the CPRA. In its June 8, 2023 Report, the JIB recommended the PHP 50,000 fine with a stern warning, but the dismissal of the charge against him as a member of the Bar.
issues: Whether Judge Asuncion is administratively liable for undue delay in deciding Civil Case No. 12-9697, and for what offense.
What penalty should be imposed, considering his prior administrative liability.
Whether he is also liable as a member of the Bar under the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability.
ruling:
**1. Yes, he is guilty of simple neglect of duty.** In administrative cases the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence, meaning relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion, and the complainant did so. Simple neglect of duty is the failure to give proper attention to an expected task, signifying a disregard of duty resulting from carelessness or indifference. The complainant completed his evidence and memorandum in 2018, and his exhibits were ruled on by April 11, 2019, yet the decision came only on March 24, 2023, "three years and two months after the complainant filed the Motion for a Decision." "Even if a period of one year is removed in due consideration of the pandemic," the decision was rendered beyond the three-month period of Article VIII, Section 15(1). The judge did not deny the delay. His excuses may be valid reasons, but he never sought an extension, as OCA Circular No. 243-2022 allows, and regular court operations had long resumed when he decided the case. **His argument that the complainant should have used judicial remedies against the decision deserved "scant consideration": the crux of the case is the inordinate delay, not the merits.**

**2. A fine of PHP 50,000.** Simple neglect of duty is a less serious offense punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 but not exceeding PHP 100,000 (Rule 140, Section 15(b), in relation to Section 17(2)). His earlier reprimand for undue delay in RTJ-20-2592 is an aggravating circumstance under Section 19, and Section 20 allows a penalty of up to double the maximum when aggravating circumstances are present. The Court found a fine of PHP 50,000 appropriate and added a stern warning.

**3. No liability as a member of the Bar.** The Court agreed with the JIB that there was no evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rule that would make him liable under the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath.
disposition: The JIB's June 8, 2023 Report and Recommendation was ADOPTED in full. Judge Miguel S. Asuncion was found GUILTY of simple neglect of duty and FINED PHP 50,000, payable within three months from promulgation, and was STERNLY WARNED that a repetition of the same offense would be dealt with more severely. The complaint against him as a member of the Philippine Bar was DISMISSED for lack of merit.

bar_questions.q: A civil case pending before RTC Judge Ramos was submitted for decision on February 1, 2022. The plaintiff filed motions for early decision in 2022 and 2023, but Judge Ramos decided the case only in September 2024. Charged administratively, he explained that he had a heavy caseload, served as executive judge, attended courtesy calls with local officials, and had a family member who was ill. He never asked the Supreme Court for an extension of time. Is he administratively liable? If so, for what offense?

alac.answer: Yes. He is liable for simple neglect of duty for undue delay in rendering a decision.
alac.legal_basis: Lower courts must decide cases within three months from submission (Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 15(1)). Undue delay in rendering a decision is a form of negligence classified as gross or simple neglect of duty under Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. A judge who cannot decide within the period must ask for an extension through the OCA (OCA Circular No. 243-2022). Heavy caseload, duties as executive judge, courtesy calls and family health concerns do not excuse the delay where no extension was sought. Simple neglect of duty is a less serious charge punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 but not exceeding PHP 100,000. (Francisco v. Judge Asuncion, A.M. No. RTJ-26-119, November 5, 2025)
alac.application: Judge Ramos had until about May 1, 2022 to decide, but he did so more than two years later. His reasons might have justified an extension, but he never asked for one, so they cannot excuse the delay after the fact. The delay shows a failure to give proper attention to a task expected of him, which is simple neglect of duty. Absent other circumstances, the penalty is suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 up to PHP 100,000.
alac.conclusion: Judge Ramos is guilty of simple neglect of duty and may be suspended or fined within the range for a less serious charge.

bar_questions.q: Same facts as above, but (i) Judge Ramos argues that the complaint should be dismissed because he has already decided the case and the complainant's proper remedy is to appeal; and (ii) the records show that he was previously fined for a similar delay. (a) Rule on his argument. (b) How does the prior fine affect the penalty?

alac.answer: (a) The argument fails because the charge concerns the delay, not the merits of the decision. (b) The prior fine is an aggravating circumstance that allows the Court to impose a suspension or fine of up to double the maximum.
alac.legal_basis: In an administrative case for undue delay, the crux is the inordinate delay, not the merits of the decision, so the availability of judicial remedies against the decision does not bar the complaint. Under Rule 140, Section 19, a previous administrative liability for which a penalty was imposed, whatever its nature or gravity, is an aggravating circumstance. Under Section 20, when aggravating circumstances are present, the Court may impose a suspension or fine not exceeding double the prescribed maximum. (Francisco v. Judge Asuncion, A.M. No. RTJ-26-119, November 5, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The complaint does not ask whether Judge Ramos decided correctly; it charges him with deciding years late. Rendering the decision afterward, and the complainant's right to appeal it, do not erase the delay. (b) Because he was previously fined, an aggravating circumstance is present, so the Court may go beyond the ordinary maximum for simple neglect of duty, up to double it. The Court still has discretion to impose a fine within the ordinary range; in Francisco it found PHP 50,000 appropriate despite a prior reprimand.
alac.conclusion: Judge Ramos remains liable despite having decided the case, and his prior fine aggravates his liability.

bar_questions.q: In the same case, the complainant asks that Judge Ramos also be fined as a member of the Bar for violating the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, since every lawyer must be diligent. The only evidence offered is the delay itself. (a) Should the Court impose a separate penalty on him as a lawyer? (b) What quantum of proof does the complainant need in this administrative case?

alac.legal_basis: A judge found liable for undue delay is not separately liable as a member of the Bar under the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath absent evidence of corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules. In administrative cases, the complainant must prove the charge by substantial evidence: relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to justify a conclusion. The standard is met when there is reasonable ground to believe the respondent is responsible, even if the evidence is not overwhelming or preponderant. (Francisco v. Judge Asuncion, A.M. No. RTJ-26-119, November 5, 2025)
alac.application: (a) The only proof is the delay, which is already penalized as simple neglect of duty. Nothing shows corruption, an intent to violate the law, or a flagrant disregard of rules, so no separate penalty as a lawyer is warranted. (b) The complainant need only present substantial evidence of the delay, which the court records themselves supply.
alac.conclusion: Judge Ramos should be penalized only for simple neglect of duty, which the complainant can establish by substantial evidence.

notes: The decision applied Canon 6, Section 5 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct and Rule 140 as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. It did not cite the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC), on which the 2027 judicial ethics syllabus is based. The decision did not state the exact date the case was deemed submitted for decision; it measured the delay from the Motion for a Decision of January 7, 2020.
